name: Dana Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good afternoon, Dana, and thank you for your time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential. What's a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach Year 2 at Holy Trinity, a small church primary school in a market town, and this is my second year. Twenty-four six- and seven-year-olds: assembly, phonics, maths, reading with each child in turn, and the afternoon is topic or art. I love Friday celebration assembly, when a shy child gets a certificate and looks for their mum in the back row. I find the planning hard, honestly, because I still take ages and my head teacher sends my plans back with red pen.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Daniel, who's a joiner, and we're getting married at our church next summer. We bought a little cottage last year with help from my parents, and I've still got about eight months of savings on top. I don't use AI at all and I don't want to. I believe in hard work, family and doing things properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, because children need people, not machines. I'd say it to the other teachers and at church. I wouldn't put anything online; I don't really use social media for opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it just means I keep doing my job the way I was trained. The real thing I worry about is my planning, and whether I'll get through my next lesson observation without the red pen. AI wouldn't fix that anyway; practice would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd ask Mrs Pemberton, my head teacher, if I could watch the Year 1 teacher plan a week, because she's brilliant at it. We'd keep saving for the wedding and pay a bit extra off the cottage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the red pen. How does that feel day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It stings, but my head teacher is fair, and she's usually right. Last week she circled a maths lesson where I'd planned forty minutes of work for a twenty-minute slot. I know I'll get there. My mum was a teacher, and she said the first three years are the hardest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything outside AI that worries you about the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small schools like ours get merged when numbers drop, and our roll is a bit lower this year. If Holy Trinity merged with the big school in town, I'd lose the feel of the place. But there are plenty of schools round here, so I'd still have work.

I'd say it to colleagues and at **church**, but not online.
think: I'd keep teaching the way I was **trained**.
My real worry is **planning** and my next lesson observation.
do: Ask to watch the **Year 1 teacher** plan a full week.
Pay a little **extra** off the cottage.

fieldNote: Her pressure is **planning skill**, which she trusts practice to fix.
A dropping **school roll** is a quiet worry unrelated to AI.
Her values centre on **family, church** and doing things properly.

steps.text: Watch the Year 1 teacher plan a full week
Overpay the cottage mortgage a little each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be careful what we let into classrooms. I'd say families and churches should have a say, not just tech firms and the government. I'd say it at the parents' evening if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job would change but not disappear. Six-year-olds need someone to tie their shoes and hear them read, and a little church school like ours would be slow to change. But the planning, marking and reports could all go onto software, and I'd be made to use it, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the training if the school made it compulsory, and no more. I'd keep planning by hand where I'm allowed to. We'd carry on with the wedding and the cottage; I wouldn't change our plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not frightened, just a bit sad that the job is turning into screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be made to use it. What if you refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd look for a school that let me teach my way, maybe an independent church school. There are a few within half an hour. I'd rather move to another school than be told to plan lessons with a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech companies, mostly, for selling it to schools as a miracle. And the government, for wanting things cheap. Parents never asked for this.

feel: **Uneasy** and a bit **sad** the job is turning into screens.
S1.quote: I'd rather move to another school than be told to plan lessons with a machine.
fieldNote: She'd **move schools** rather than change how she plans.

Her life plans stay **fixed**: wedding and cottage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities would have to pull together, because the government can't fix this. I'd say children need teachers with values, not software. I'd say it plainly at church and at school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd lose my job or most of it. If AI can plan, teach and mark better than me by 2028, a school will put a screen at the front and keep one adult, probably a teaching assistant, to look after the children till the robots come in 2031. I'm junior, I'm slow, and I won't use the tools, so I'd be among the first to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop overpaying the cottage and hold our savings as cash. I'd talk to Daniel about leaning on his joinery for a while, since hands-on work lasts longer. Parents will still want a person they trust with their little ones, so I'd look into childminding from home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, because we've got the cottage and savings, but frightened for what teaching becomes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government help if you lost your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I had to. I'd rather work, even childminding, than live on handouts. My family would help first, and the church would too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Daniel the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll be all right because we've got each other and the cottage. And I'd ask him to teach me some joinery, half joking. He'd laugh, but he'd do it.

I'd say children need **teachers with values**.

S2.quote: Parents will still want a person they trust with their little ones, so I'd look into childminding from home.
fieldNote: She sees herself as **first to go** and says so calmly.
Her fallback is **family, church** and childminding, not benefits.
Her fiancé's **hands-on work** buys the household time.

steps.text: Stop overpaying the cottage and keep savings in cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives families, churches and schools time to plan sensibly. I'd say we should teach children manners, faith and hard work, things a machine can't. I'd say it to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years helps, but it doesn't change where it ends. By 2031 the thinking side of teaching would be gone, and I'd be twenty-nine with a few years' experience. The hands-on care lasts till 2034, so I'd want to be in a job that's mostly that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to move to Reception, where it's more care and less paper. I'd get my childminding registration done as a backup in the next couple of years. We'd still get married next summer; I wouldn't let this touch the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. I like having time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI tools with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know that might cost me, but I've seen what screens do to children's attention, so I'd rather be the teacher who doesn't use one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change plans for children of your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We want children soon after the wedding. If anything this makes me want to stay home with them for a few years. Family comes first, whatever the machines do.

I'd say schools should teach **manners, faith** and hard work.

S3.quote: I've seen what screens do to children's attention, so I'd rather be the teacher who doesn't use one.
fieldNote: She'd **shift to Reception**, where care outweighs paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this the right way, with families in charge, not the tech firms. I'd say it calmly. There's time for common sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right for most of it. I'd probably have young children at home by 2036 and might be teaching part time anyway. The care side of teaching lasts till robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on teaching and get better at planning the old way. I'd keep paying off the cottage faster. I wouldn't do anything dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's there, but it's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want the government to do anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep its hands off how small schools teach, mostly. And make sure apprenticeships and trades are well funded, because people like Daniel will be needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children, really. Children will grow up with machines answering everything, and I'd want them to still learn to read a proper book. And to say thank you.

I'd say there's time for **common sense** in schools and at home.
think: I'd likely have **young children** and teach part time by 2036.
The **care side** of teaching lasts till robots around 2039.
do: Keep teaching and improve **planning the old way**.
Do **nothing dramatic** with our savings or the wedding.
S4.quote: Children will grow up with machines answering everything, and I'd want them to still learn to read a proper book.
fieldNote: A long runway lets her **traditional plans** proceed.
She wants government to **stay out** of small schools but fund trades.
Her worry turns to **children's habits**, not her pay.

steps.text: Keep teaching Year 2 and practising planning by hand

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be one of the first teachers to go. What would help is schools being allowed to keep human teachers if parents want them, and support for people setting up things like childminding.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about faith. A machine can teach a child to read, but it can't pray with a child who's lost a grandparent. That's part of my job too, in a church school.
